blocks.p: Then he went on until he came to the house of the Interpreter, where he knocked again and again. At last someone came to the door and asked who was there.
“Sir,” said Christian, “here is a traveler who was told by an acquaintance of the master of this house to call here for my good. So I would like to speak with the master of the house.”
So the servant called for the master of the house, who after a little while came to Christian and asked what he wanted.

“Sir,” said Christian, “I am a man who has come from the City of Destruction and am going to Mount Zion; and I was told by the man who stands at the gate at the head of this road that if I called here, you would show me excellent things, things that would help me on my journey.”
“Come in,” said the Interpreter. “I will show you what will do you good.”

So he told his servant to light the candle, and told Christian to follow him. He took him into a private room and had his servant open a door; and when he had done so, Christian saw a picture of a very grave person hanging on the wall. This is what it looked like: its eyes were lifted up to heaven; the best of books was in its hand; the law of truth was written on its lips; the world was behind its back. It stood as if it were pleading with men, and a crown of gold hung over its head.
“What does this mean?” said Christian.

“The man in this picture is one in a thousand,” said the Interpreter. “He can father children [1 Cor. 4:15], labor in birth with children [Gal. 4:19], and nurse them himself once they are born. You see him with his eyes lifted up to heaven, the best of books in his hand, and the law of truth written on his lips: that is to show you that his work is to know dark things and to make them plain to sinners; and so you see him standing as if he pleaded with men. You see the world cast behind him and a crown hanging over his head: that is to show you that, because he slights and despises the things of the present out of love for his Master’s service, he is sure to have glory for his reward in the world to come.

“I have shown you this picture first,” the Interpreter went on, “because the man in it is the only man whom the Lord of the place you are going to has authorized to be your guide in all the difficult places you may meet along the way. So pay close attention to what I have shown you, and keep firmly in mind what you have seen, in case on your journey you meet some who pretend to lead you right, but whose road goes down to death.”

Then he took him by the hand and led him into a very large parlor that was full of dust, because it had never been swept. When they had looked at it a little while, the Interpreter called for a man to sweep it. But as soon as he began to sweep, the dust flew up so thickly that Christian almost choked on it. Then the Interpreter said to a young woman standing nearby, “Bring the water here and sprinkle the room.” When she had done so, the room was swept and cleaned with ease.
“What does this mean?” said Christian.

“This parlor,” the Interpreter answered, “is the heart of a man who was never made holy by the sweet grace of the gospel. The dust is his original sin and the inner corruption that has defiled the whole man. The one who began to sweep first is the Law; but she who brought the water and sprinkled it is the Gospel. Now, you saw that as soon as the first began to sweep, the dust flew about so much that he could not clean the room, and you were almost choked. That is to show you that the law, instead of cleansing the heart from sin by its working, actually revives sin, strengthens it, and increases it in the soul, even while it exposes and forbids it; for the law does not give the power to overcome it. [Rom. 7:6; 1 Cor. 15:56; Rom. 5:20]

“Then you saw the young woman sprinkle the room with water, and it was cleaned with ease. That is to show you that when the gospel comes into the heart with its sweet and precious influence, then, just as you saw her settle the dust by sprinkling the floor, sin is conquered and subdued, and the soul is made clean through faith in the gospel, and so made fit for the King of glory to live in.” [John 15:3; Eph. 5:26; Acts 15:9; Rom. 16:25-26; John 15:13]

Moreover, I saw in my dream that the Interpreter took him by the hand and brought him into a little room where two small children sat, each in his own chair. The older one was named Passion, and the other Patience. Passion seemed very discontented, but Patience was very quiet.
“Why is Passion so discontented?” Christian asked.
“Their guardian wants him to wait for his best things until the beginning of next year,” the Interpreter answered, “but he wants everything now. Patience is willing to wait.”

Then I saw that someone came to Passion with a bag of treasure and poured it out at his feet. He scooped it up and gloated over it, and laughed Patience to scorn. But I watched only a little while, and he had squandered it all, and had nothing left but rags.
“Explain this to me more fully,” said Christian to the Interpreter.

“These two boys are figures,” he said. “Passion stands for the people of this world, and Patience for the people of the world to come. Just as you see that Passion will have everything now, this year, that is to say, in this world, so it is with the people of this world: they must have all their good things now; they cannot wait until next year, that is, until the next world, for their share of good. The proverb ‘A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush’ carries more weight with them than all of God’s testimony about the good of the world to come. But just as you saw that he quickly squandered it all and was soon left with nothing but rags, so it will be with all such people at the end of this world.”

“Now I see that Patience has the better wisdom,” said Christian, “and for more than one reason. First, because he waits for the best things. Second, because he will have the glory of his when the other has nothing but rags.”

“Yes, and you may add another: the glory of the next world will never wear out, but these things are gone in a moment. So Passion had less reason to laugh at Patience for having his good things first than Patience will have to laugh at Passion for having his best things last. For first must give way to last, because last must have its time to come; but last gives way to nothing, for there is nothing after it. So whoever has his portion first must have a time to spend it; but whoever has his portion last will have it forever. That is why it was said to the rich man, ‘In your lifetime you received your good things, and Lazarus received bad things; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony.’” [Luke 16:25]
“Then I see it is not best to covet the things that are here now, but to wait for the things to come.”

“That is the truth. ‘For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.’ [2 Cor. 4:18] But even so, because present things and our fleshly appetites are such close neighbors, and because things to come and our physical senses are such strangers to each other, the first two become friends so quickly, and the second two stay so far apart.”

Then I saw in my dream that the Interpreter took Christian by the hand and led him to a place where a fire was burning against a wall. Someone stood beside it, constantly throwing water on it to put it out; and yet the fire burned higher and hotter.
“What does this mean?” said Christian.

“This fire is the work of grace in the heart,” the Interpreter answered. “The one who throws water on it to put it out is the Devil. But as for why the fire burns higher and hotter in spite of him, you will see the reason for that too.”
So he took him around to the other side of the wall, where he saw a man with a jar of oil in his hand, which he kept pouring into the fire, but secretly.
“What does this mean?” said Christian.

“This is Christ,” the Interpreter answered, “who with the oil of his grace continually keeps up the work he has already begun in the heart; and because of it, no matter what the devil can do, the souls of his people remain gracious still. [2 Cor. 12:9] And as for the man standing behind the wall to keep the fire going, that is to teach you that it is hard for those who are tempted to see how this work of grace is kept alive in the soul.”

I saw also that the Interpreter took him by the hand again and led him into a pleasant place where a stately palace had been built, beautiful to look at, and the sight of it delighted Christian. He also saw people walking on the top of it, clothed all in gold.
“May we go in there?” said Christian.

Then the Interpreter took him and led him up toward the door of the palace. At the door stood a great crowd of men who wanted to go in, but did not dare. A little way from the door a man sat at a table with a book and an inkwell in front of him, to take down the name of anyone who would enter. Christian also saw that the doorway was held by many men in armor, determined to do whatever harm and mischief they could to anyone who tried to get in. Christian was somewhat bewildered. At last, when every man had drawn back for fear of the armed men, Christian saw a man with a very determined face come up to the man who sat there to write, and say, “Write down my name, sir.” When that was done, Christian saw the man draw his sword, put a helmet on his head, and rush at the armed men in the doorway. They fell on him with deadly force; but the man, not discouraged in the least, set to cutting and hacking most fiercely. So after he had received and given many wounds to those who tried to keep him out, he cut his way through them all [Acts 14:22] and pressed on into the palace. Then a pleasant voice was heard from those inside, the ones walking on top of the palace, saying:
So he went in, and was clothed in garments like theirs. Then Christian smiled and said, “I think I truly know the meaning of this. Now let me go on from here.”
“No, wait,” said the Interpreter, “until I have shown you a little more; and after that you shall go on your way.”

So he took him by the hand again and led him into a very dark room, where a man sat in an iron cage. The man looked very sad. He sat with his eyes on the ground and his hands clasped together, and he sighed as if his heart would break.
“What does this mean?” said Christian.
The Interpreter told him to talk with the man.
“What are you?” Christian asked him.
“I am what I once was not.”
“What were you once?”

“I once made a fine and flourishing profession of faith,” the man said, “both in my own eyes and in the eyes of others. I once was, as I thought, well on the way to the Celestial City, and I even felt joy at the thought that I would get there.” [Luke 8:13]
“Well, but what are you now?”
“Now I am a man of despair, and I am shut up in it, as in this iron cage. I cannot get out. Oh, now I cannot!”
“But how did you come to this condition?”

“I stopped keeping watch and being sober-minded. I gave my desires free rein. I sinned against the light of the Word and the goodness of God. I have grieved the Spirit, and he is gone. I tempted the devil, and he has come to me. I have provoked God to anger, and he has left me. I have so hardened my heart that I cannot repent.”
Then Christian said to the Interpreter, “But is there no hope for a man like this?”
“Ask him,” said the Interpreter.
“No, sir,” said Christian, “please, you ask him.”
“Is there no hope,” said the Interpreter, “except that you must be kept in the iron cage of despair?”
“No, none at all.”
“Why, the Son of the Blessed One is full of compassion.”

“I have crucified him all over again [Heb. 6:6]; I have despised his person [Luke 19:14]; I have despised his righteousness; I have ‘treated his blood as an unholy thing’; I have ‘insulted the Spirit of grace.’ [Heb. 10:28-29] So I have shut myself out of all the promises, and now nothing is left to me but threats, dreadful threats, terrifying threats, of certain judgment and raging fire that will consume me as an enemy.”
“What did you bring yourself into this condition for?”
“For the lusts, pleasures, and profits of this world, in which I promised myself great delight. But now every one of those things bites me and gnaws at me like a burning worm.”
“But can’t you repent now, and turn back?”

“God has denied me repentance. His Word gives me no encouragement to believe. Yes, he himself has shut me up in this iron cage, and all the men in the world cannot let me out. O eternity, eternity! How will I bear the misery I must face in eternity!”
Then the Interpreter said to Christian, “Remember this man’s misery, and let it be a warning to you forever.”

“Well,” said Christian, “this is frightening! God help me to keep watch and be sober-minded, and to pray that I may avoid what caused this man’s misery! Sir, isn’t it time for me to go on my way now?”
“Wait until I show you one more thing, and then you shall go on your way.”
So he took Christian by the hand again and led him into a bedroom where someone was getting out of bed; and as he put on his clothes, he shook and trembled.
“Why is this man trembling like this?” said Christian.
The Interpreter told the man to explain to Christian why he was doing so. So he began:

“Last night, as I slept, I dreamed; and I saw the sky grow utterly black. It thundered and lightened so terribly that I was in agony. So I looked up in my dream and saw the clouds racing at an unusual rate. Then I heard a great sound of a trumpet, and saw a man sitting on a cloud, attended by the thousands of heaven. They were all in flaming fire, and the sky itself was ablaze. Then I heard a voice saying, ‘Arise, you dead, and come to judgment!’ And with that the rocks split, the graves opened, and the dead in them came out. Some of them were overjoyed and looked upward; and some tried to hide themselves under the mountains. [1 Cor. 15:52; 1 Thess. 4:16; Jude 14; John 5:28-29; 2 Thess. 1:7-8; Rev. 20:11-14; Isa. 26:21; Micah 7:16-17; Ps. 95:1-3; Dan. 7:10] Then I saw the man who sat on the cloud open the book and call the world to come near. Yet because of a fierce flame that came out from before him, there was a fitting distance between him and them, like the distance between the judge and the prisoners at the bar. [Mal. 3:2-3; Dan. 7:9-10] I also heard it proclaimed to those who attended the man on the cloud: ‘Gather the weeds, the chaff, and the stubble, and throw them into the burning lake.’ [Matt. 3:12; 13:30; Mal. 4:1] And with that the bottomless pit opened, right about where I stood, and out of its mouth poured smoke and coals of fire, with hideous noises. And it was said to the same attendants, ‘Gather my wheat into the barn.’ [Luke 3:17] With that I saw many caught up and carried away into the clouds; but I was left behind. [1 Thess. 4:16-17] I tried to hide myself too, but I could not, for the man who sat on the cloud kept his eye on me. My sins came into my mind, and my conscience accused me on every side. [Rom. 3:14-15] At that I woke up.”
“But what was it about this sight that made you so afraid?”

“Why, I thought the day of judgment had come and that I was not ready for it. But what frightened me most was that the angels gathered up so many and left me behind; and that the pit of hell opened its mouth right where I stood. My conscience tormented me too; and, as I thought, the Judge kept his eye on me the whole time, with indignation in his face.”
Then the Interpreter said to Christian, “Have you considered all these things?”
“Yes, and they fill me with both hope and fear.”
“Well, keep all these things in your mind so that they may be like a goad in your side, to prod you forward on the road you must take.”
Then Christian tightened his belt and set himself to his journey.
“May the Comforter always be with you, good Christian,” said the Interpreter, “to guide you on the road that leads to the City.”
So Christian went on his way, saying:

v: Here I have seen things rare and profitable,
things pleasant, dreadful, things to make me stable
in what I have begun to take in hand.
So let me think on them, and understand
the reason they were shown me, and stay true,
and thankful, good Interpreter, to you.
